newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy goverment readies Easter budget blitz.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy goverment readies Easter budget blitz.

text.p: The Italian government announced on Friday it would slash a further 15.5 trillion lire ($9.2 billion) off the deficit in an Easter budget blitz aimed at priming the economy for the single European currency.

Cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli told reporters that latest data from the first three months of the year pointed to the public administration deficit hitting 3.8 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
The Maastricht Treaty demands a deficit/GDP ratio of three percent for countries wishing to sign up to planned European economic and monetary union (EMU) when it is launched in 1999.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has pledged to do everything needed to ensure that Italy meets the tough Maastricht target and Micheli said the latest round of budget rigour would be introduced before Easter, which falls on March 30.
"All our options over the budget remain open...it will be a just budget," Micheli said.
The government introduced a hefty 62.5 trillion lire budget only last December, hoping that this would be enough to cut the deficit to three percent of GDP from 6.7 percent in 1996.

But an unexpected surge in spending late last year, coupled with a sluggish economy, have forced the Treasury to re-do its sums. Micheli said the economy was expected to grow 1.2-1.4 percent this year against a previously forecast 2.0 percent.

After five years of increasingly stringent cutbacks, Prodi's options are now limited and he is likely to run into stiff opposition from business leaders as well as trades unions over this latest round of belt tightening.
He also faces a fight with a parliamentary ally, the hardleft Communist Refoundation, over the budget package.
Refoundation holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament and is the first major party in pro-Europe Italy openly to question EMU.
"It's clear the government has now decided to present Italians with this (budget) Easter present," Oliviero Diliberto, the lower house leader of Refoundation, said in a statement.
"A mini-budget is completely useless, but we are willing to discuss it on merit...on the understanding that we cannot accept new taxes, or, above all, cuts to social spending," he added.
Refoundation's rigid stance against reduced expenditure on the welfare state has left Prodi looking elsewhere for cash.
Most analysts expect the government to raise up to seven trillion lire by simply transfering severance payment funds, currently held by companies, into Treasury coffers.
Italian industry uses this large reserve of money for their cash flow. If they were deprived of it, they would be forced to seek expensive loans from the inefficient banking sector.

Giorgio Fossa, the leader of industrialists' organisation Confindustria, said such a measure belonged to a "predatory culture" and urged the government to talk to business leaders before ploughing ahead with the budget.
"If there are no talks, if there is a dialogue of the deaf, nothing positive will come from it," Fossa told a conference.
He added that if the centre-left government was really serious about getting state accounts in order, it would have to introduce some structural changes to welfare spending.
"I realise you can't cut 15 trillion lire from the welfare state overnight, but you have to start, you have to send a signal," he said. $1= 1,692 lire
